Students tackled the range of questions well especially in Section B's verbal answers which have proved to be the most demanding questions in previous series. As in previous series, students must be reminded of the following key techniques: - listen carefully to whole utterances before putting down an answer. - in verbal answers in English, write down exactly what you hear. Teachers are reminded that students are required to write four sentences about what is in the photo, i.e. a phrase that contains a verb or a construction using voici or voilà. Each sentence is marked separately and is worth a maximum of two marks. The best responses included successful use of simple phrases such as ‘’il y a or ‘voici/voilà’. Where students failed to score marks, it was mainly for the following reasons:

• Ambiguous use of numbers e.g. ‘il y a un quatre personnes’. • When students attempted longer, more complex responses e.g. ‘il y a deux garçons et ils amusant’ • Not including a verb or issues with verb formation which caused delay in communication e.g. use of the infinitive form of a verb or use of an auxiliary verb with an infinitive. • Although it is acceptable for the students to put themselves in the photo and sentences such as ‘je regarde mon ordinateur’ are credited, giving an opinion e.g. ‘j’aime mon ordinateur’ does not describe what is in the photo and is not credited. • Incomprehensible spelling of key vocabulary and English words that do not exist in French.

Advice to students

• Keep the sentences simple to ensure that a clear message is being communicated. • Avoid adding a variety of details to individual sentences.

Teachers are reminded that there are 10 marks for Content and 6 marks for Quality of Language. Students are required to write approximately 40 words in total about four different bullet points. All bullet points are compulsory and must be covered, but there is no need for equal coverage of the bullets.

4 of 9

Content The criteria for assessment refer to both the coverage of the bullet points and clarity of communication. The vast majority of candidates understood the need to address all bullet points with some development. The first two bullet points ‘la musique’ and ‘la télévision’ were topics that were widely known and were successfully addressed. The third bullet point ‘votre santé’ was less widely known, although many students were able to address the bullet point effectively by including information with an opinion that communicated. The final bullet point ‘votre dîner préféré’ was addressed successfully in general although some students wrote sentences using ‘votre’ for this bullet point and the previous bullet point ‘votre santé’ which could not be credited.

Quality of language

The majority of students were able to include a good variety of appropriate vocabulary and grammatical structures. Students demonstrated an ability to include different ways of expressing opinions, different persons of the verb and the use of intensifiers and connectives. The majority of students were also able to produce responses that were generally accurate and were able to access the top band of marks. Teachers are reminded that for the highest marks, complex sentences need to be handled with confidence. However, as in previous series, there were still many students who included templated formulaic complex sentences and/or idiomatic expressions and either overused the same phrases, used them inappropriately or had not been able to reproduce them accurately thereby producing complex structures that could not be considered to be successful.

Accuracy

The criteria for assessment makes reference to verbs and tense formations, and the different types of errors made by students. Teachers are reminded that ‘major’ errors are those that create a delay or breakdown in communication, and ‘minor’ errors, although they are still inaccuracies, do not. As in previous series, the majority of students were able to produce work worthy of 3 marks and above. Major errors were mainly inaccurate tense formations and/or the inappropriate use of infinitives. As always, minor errors seen included errors of gender, inaccurate adjectival agreements and prepositions, omissions and minor misspellings.

Content

Students approached this question well, with many able to produce extended pieces of writing with developed responses. They were aware of the need to refer to the three time frames and express at least two opinions and, for the most part were successful in achieving this. The criteria for assessment for Content focus on four elements: coverage of the bullet points, development of ideas, clarity of communication and expression of opinions. Inaccuracy and therefore lack of clarity of communication (referred to as ‘lapses’) impacted negatively on marks awarded.

Question 1.1 Bullet point 1 ‘votre petit job’ was very accessible to students, and they were able to produce extended responses. Bullet point 2 ‘votre opinion du travail’ was also well-covered, as students are very familiar with this type of bullet point. Although Bullet point 3 ‘vos activités récemment au travail’ provided students with the opportunity to produce an account using past time frames, some students did not spot the time marker ‘récemment’ and did not reference the past. Bullet point 4 ‘votre préférence pour le travail à l’avenir’ presented no difficulties for students, and they were able to cover the bullet point well.

Question 1.2 This was the more popular choice with students as it covered topics with which they are more familiar. Bullet point 1 ‘ce que vous mangez’ provided students with the opportunity to produce well- developed responses. Bullet point 2 ‘votre opinion du sport’ was also well-covered, as students are very familiar with this type of bullet point. Bullet point 3 ‘une activité sportive le week-end dernier’ created no difficulty for students, who were able to produce a coherent account referencing past activities. Bullet point 4 ‘votre style de vie à l’avenir’ was well-covered. Some students, however, wrote about general future plans without it being clear that these were ‘lifestyle’ choices.

Quality of language The key features of the criteria for assessment here are variety of language, attempts at complexity, time frames and accuracy. Examples of work including variety and complexity of language included: different persons of the verb, different ways of expressing likes and dislikes, infinitive constructions, a variety of adjectives, connectives, intensifiers, negatives, the use of subordinate clauses, relative pronouns, and a variety of tenses including subjunctives. Less successful language included inaccurate tense formation and minor errors such as omissions, errors of gender, adjectival agreement and singular/plural confusion.
